The Yalkut Shimoni and Its Place in Jewish History
The source surveys the monumental work of Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan of Frankfurt, who in the 13th century composed the Yalkut Shimoni, a wide-ranging anthology that gathers thousands of midrashim arranged according to the order of the verses of the Bible. The text emphasises that this work is not merely a technical collection, but a "national archive" that preserved rare textual versions and lost works which, were it not for the author's sophisticated work of collecting and editing, would have been entirely forgotten. Through the analysis of the architectural and methodological structure of the book, the figure of Rabbi Shimon emerges as an **"architect of Jewish memory"**, who acted out of an urge to rescue the spiritual treasures of the Sages in a period of persecutions and frequent political changes. Beyond its bibliographical value, the article connects the fruits of the labour of the "head of the preachers" with the continuity of the Torah tradition in Ashkenaz, as expressed in the legacy of the Adler family and in the rulings of the great sages of later generations.
The Torah Teaching and Historical Work of Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan of Frankfurt: A Comprehensive Analysis of the Yalkut Shimoni and Its Place in Jewish History
The monumental midrashic work known as the "Yalkut Shimoni" constitutes one of the most significant and influential contributions to the Torah literature of the Middle Ages. At the head of this enterprise stood Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan of Frankfurt, a figure who earned the title "head of the preachers", and who succeeded in collecting and editing thousands of sayings of the Sages into a systematic anthology accompanying the whole of Scripture.[1, 2] The importance of the Yalkut goes beyond its being an aid to the learner; it serves as a national archive in which rare textual versions and lost midrashim were preserved which, were it not for Rabbi Shimon's work, would have been utterly forgotten.[2] A thorough analysis of his Torah teaching requires a combined examination of the historical background in 13th-century Frankfurt, his distinctive editorial method, and the protracted scholarly controversy over his identity and his period.[3, 4]
The Historical and Social Background of Frankfurt Jewry in the 13th Century
To understand the motives behind the writing of the Yalkut, one must examine the complex reality of the Jews of Ashkenaz in the 13th century. The Frankfurt community was at that time at the height of its spiritual flourishing, but also under the constant threat of political and religious upheavals. Evidence of the existence of an organised community in Frankfurt exists from as early as the beginning of the 12th century, as can be learned from the writings of the Raavan.[5] The Jews of the city enjoyed a special legal status of "protected Jews" or "servants of the royal chamber" (Servi Camerae Regis), a status that guaranteed them royal protection in return for heavy payments, but also defined them as a foreign element in German feudal society.[6]
Within this reality, the relative calm that prevailed in Frankfurt until the middle of the 13th century enabled Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan to undertake his mighty enterprise of collection. The scholar Y. L. Zunz estimated that only in such a period, of relative calm and security, would it have been possible to hold so extensive a library and to conduct so complex a process of copying and editing.[2, 4] This situation changed tragically in the year 1241, in the event known as the "Judenschlacht" (the slaughter of the Jews), in which about 159 of the Jews of the community were murdered and the whole community was temporarily destroyed.[5, 6] This destruction highlights Rabbi Shimon's work as that of one who sought to preserve the treasures of the past just before the storm. The Yalkut Shimoni reflects the Ashkenazi attempt to "rescue" the literature of the Sages and to make it accessible to future generations at a time when persecutions and wanderings endangered the continuity of study.[2, 7]
The Controversy over the Identity and Date of Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan
One of the central topics in the bibliographical research of the Middle Ages is the question of the identity of the author of the Yalkut. The primary source linking the name Rabbi Shimon with the work is a scribe's note in an Oxford manuscript from the year 1308.[2] Nevertheless, the exact identity remained the subject of fierce dispute among the scholars of the "Wissenschaft des Judentums" in the 19th century.
Shir (Shlomo Yehuda Rapoport) sought to date the Yalkut earlier, to the beginning of the 11th century, identifying its author as Rabbi Shimon Kara, the father of the famous biblical commentator Rabbi Yosef Kara.[2, 4] Rapoport based his view on mentions of "Rabbi Shimon" in Rashi's commentaries and on the linguistic similarity between the epithets "Kara" and "Darshan", both of which attest to expertise in Scripture and in Midrash.[4, 7] Against this, Avraham Epstein and Y. L. Zunz proved that this identification does not stand up to criticism. They showed that Rashi and the author of the "Arukh" did not know the Yalkut at all as a consolidated work, and that Rabbi Yosef Kara himself never quoted from this work in his many commentaries.[2, 3]
The decisive proof that the Yalkut belongs to the later period of the 13th century is the use of late midrashim such as "Devarim Rabbah" and "Midrash Tadshe", which did not exist in the time of R. Shimon Kara.[2] Moreover, linguistic studies have shown that the author of the Yalkut incorporated into it passages from Rashi's commentary on the Talmud word for word, which proves beyond all doubt that he was active after Rashi's time.[2, 4] Accordingly, the conclusion accepted today is that the author is Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan of Frankfurt, who lived and worked at the beginning of the 13th century, and the title "head of the preachers" was conferred on him because of the enormous reputation he acquired as the possessor of the most comprehensive knowledge of the midrashim of the Sages.[2, 8]
The Architectural Structure of the Yalkut Shimoni
The Yalkut is divided into two main parts, covering the whole of the Bible, with each part maintaining an internal structure of "remazim" (numbered sections).[3, 7] This division is not merely technical but reflects an overall conception of Scripture as an organic text in which every word can serve as an opening to an entire world of homilies.
Part One: The Torah
This part comprises 963 remazim divided according to the books of the Five Books of the Torah. It can be seen that the internal division is adapted to the extent of the midrashim available on each book:
The Book of Genesis: §§ 1–162. This book is rich in cosmological aggadic midrashim and in the stories of the patriarchs.[7]
The Book of Exodus: §§ 163–427. Here the emphasis shifts to halakhic midrashim (the Mekhilta) alongside the aggadot of the redemption.[7]
The Book of Leviticus: §§ 428–682. The main sources here are from the Sifra (Torat Kohanim).[7]
The Book of Numbers: §§ 683–788. A combination of Sifrei Bamidbar and Midrash Rabbah.[7]
The Book of Deuteronomy: §§ 789–963. The closing of the midrashic circle with Sifrei Devarim and late midrashim.[7]
Part Two: Prophets and Writings
This part comprises 1085 remazim and is arranged according to the original order of the books as it appears in the baraita in tractate Bava Batra 14b.[3] Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan preserved the ancient midrashic order in which Jeremiah and Ezekiel precede Isaiah, although later printers changed the order to conform to the accepted one.[2, 3] An especially impressive achievement is the treatment of the books of the "Writings" such as Psalms, Job and Proverbs, for which Rabbi Shimon collected homilies from hundreds of different sources in order to create an exegetical sequence on each and every verse.[3, 7]
The Editorial Methodology and Homiletical Teaching of Rabbi Shimon
Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan was not merely a copyist, but a sophisticated editor with a defined exegetical conception. He worked according to a principle of "maximal collection" on the one hand, and "relevant filtering" on the other.[2] His editorial method included several distinctive features that made the Yalkut a powerful tool of study:
Preservation of the original language: unlike other compilers who reworked the midrashim into their personal style, Rabbi Shimon took care to preserve the original language – Hebrew, Babylonian or Galilean Aramaic.[2] This makes the Yalkut a most reliable source for the textual criticism of the literature of the Sages.[2]
Abridgement and division of homilies: when a long homily contained references to several verses, Rabbi Shimon did not hesitate to divide it and to place each passage in its relevant place in the Torah or in the Prophets and Writings.[7] In cases where he wished to save space, he cited only the beginning of the homily and referred the learner to another place where it appears in full.[7]
References and placement of sources: in the first printings (Salonika), the source references appeared within the text itself, which attests to the scholarly transparency that Rabbi Shimon sought to apply to his work.[3, 7] The printers in Venice moved the sources to the margins, a change that modern scholars regard as a certain impairment of the original character of the work.[7]
The index of verses: recent research has discovered in manuscripts an "index of verses" that apparently served as a draft for the editorial work.[2] This index enabled Rabbi Shimon to see which verses had already been "covered" by certain homilies and to avoid unnecessary duplications, which attests to a systematic and modern approach to the editing of information.[2]
The use of the term "midrash" in the Yalkut is sometimes general, but in certain places it is very specific. For example, in the books of Samuel and Psalms, the term "midrash" always refers to the specific midrash on that book.[7] Rabbi Shimon's ability to navigate among dozens of works and to find the most suitable homily for each exegetical context justly earned him the title "head of the preachers".[2]
The Archive of Lost Midrashim: His Contribution to the Preservation of the Literature of the Sages
One of the most fascinating aspects of Rabbi Shimon's work is the rescue of entire works that were lost to the world and survived only as quotations within the Yalkut. For the world of Torah and of scholarship, the Yalkut is a kind of "Noah's ark" of the Midrash.[2]
Midrash Avkir is the most prominent example. It is an ancient midrash on the books of Genesis and Exodus, which today is not in our possession as an independent work.[9] Everything we know about it, including the wondrous legends about the angels Shemhazai and Azael, was preserved thanks to Rabbi Shimon's meticulous compiling.[10] Similar importance attaches to Midrash Va-Yisau, which describes the wars of the sons of Jacob, and to the Alphabet of Ben Sira, extensive passages of which were incorporated into the Yalkut.[7, 10]
Beyond the preservation of lost works, the Yalkut helps in reconstructing the original versions of existing midrashim. Since Rabbi Shimon used early Ashkenazi manuscripts, his quotations sometimes reflect a more accurate text than the one found in the later printings of "Midrash Rabbah", which underwent changes due to censorship.[2] The ability to compare the text of the Yalkut with the text of the midrashim before us is a basic working tool for every Torah scholar and researcher of Midrash today.[2, 3]
The Spread of the Yalkut and the Vicissitudes of Its Printings
Despite its importance, the Yalkut did not become widespread immediately after it was written. Because of its enormous size, copying it was expensive and laborious, and the Jews of Ashkenaz in the 14th and 15th centuries were preoccupied with physical survival under severe persecutions.[2, 7] Only at the end of the 15th century did the book begin to appear in Spain, where it was quoted by Don Isaac Abravanel and his son Shmuel.[2, 3]
The printing revolution brought about the great breakthrough of the Yalkut into Torah consciousness:
The Salonika edition (1521-1527): the Editio Princeps (the first printing). This edition is considered the most accurate in terms of preserving the order of the sources as Rabbi Shimon established it.[2, 7]
The Venice edition (1566): edited by Rabbi Meir Prinz. This edition introduced significant changes: the transfer of the sources to the margins, the addition of explanations of difficult words ("Zayit Ra'anan") and the omission of certain passages because of Christian censorship.[2]
The Mossad HaRav Kook edition (Hyman–Shiloni): the modern scholarly edition, based on the Oxford manuscript.[8, 11] This edition restores the Yalkut to its original form through a comparison of dozens of manuscripts and early printings.[2]
His Family Lineage and the Connection with the Adler Family of Frankfurt
The figure of Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan belongs not only to the world of the book, but also to the illustrious family dynasty of Frankfurt Jewry. An ancient tradition, supported by great sages of Israel such as the Chida and the Chatam Sofer, traces the Adler (Nesher, "eagle") family to Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan.[8, 12]
The name Adler derives from the emblem that appeared on the family's house in Frankfurt, and Rabbi Natan Adler (1741−1800), one of the greatest kabbalists and halakhic authorities in Ashkenaz, is considered a direct descendant of his.[12, 13] Rabbi Natan Adler, who was the teacher of the Chatam Sofer, maintained distinctive practices such as praying in the Sephardi pronunciation and reciting the Priestly Blessing every day, practices that sometimes aroused controversy in the community but reflected the breadth of horizons of the family of the "head of the preachers".[12, 14] This connection highlights how Rabbi Shimon's teaching continued to live not only in the study halls but also within the family tradition of the sages of Frankfurt throughout the generations.[13, 15]
The Chatam Sofer himself, in his writings, frequently mentions the Yalkut Shimoni with great respect, and sees in it the foundation of his own homilies. The book "Chut ha-Meshulash" describes the pride that the Chatam Sofer felt in this lineage of his, which attests to the unchallenged authority of Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan in the Ashkenazi Torah world.[8, 14]
The Torah Worldview in the Mirror of the Yalkut
The Torah teaching of Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan is based on faith in the wholeness of the Torah. For him, the Torah is not merely a collection of commandments, but a living fabric of midrashim, stories, philosophy and halakha. This combination finds clear expression in the way he places side by side incisive halakhic sayings and profound aggadic midrashim.[3, 16]
In the portion of Devarim, for example, the Yalkut cites homilies dealing with the importance of justice and judgement. It quotes the midrash on "and I will make them heads over you" – which teaches that the standing of the leader depends on the public's recognition of him, but also on his personal responsibility towards Heaven.[16] Rabbi Shimon chooses to cite homilies that emphasise the moral aspect of public leadership, such as the warning that a judge who does not judge justly causes the Divine Presence to depart from Israel.[16]
Another area in which his teaching stands out is the attitude to the Land of Israel. Although he lived in distant Frankfurt, Rabbi Shimon meticulously collected midrashim of the Land of Israel from the Jerusalem Talmud and from the Pesikta, which express the longing for redemption and the holiness of the Land.[2, 3] His ability to bridge geographical distance and historical time in order to bring the "Torah of the Land of Israel" to the Jews of Ashkenaz is one of the hallmarks of his greatness in Torah.[2]

Where n represents the number of books of the Bible. The distribution of the remazim is not equal, and it reflects the concentration of the midrashim of the Sages in the period of the Mishnah and the Talmud:
Torah (963 remazim): constitutes about 47% of the work.
Prophets and Writings (1085 remazim): constitute about 53% of the work.
It is interesting to note that the book of Psalms alone occupies a volume of about 280 remazim (§§ 610–890), which attests to the enormous importance Rabbi Shimon attributed to this book as a basis for homilies of ethics and prayer.[7] The division of Psalms in the Yalkut (147 psalms instead of 150) reflects an ancient tradition of the Land of Israel from the period of the Amoraim, a fact that illustrates once again Rabbi Shimon's meticulousness in preserving ancient sources.[3]
Summary and Conclusions
Rabbi Shimon ha-Darshan of Frankfurt was not merely a compiler; he was an architect of Jewish memory. His work in composing the Yalkut Shimoni created a bridge across which the treasures of the Sages passed from the ancient East to the Jewry of medieval Europe and from there to the whole world.[1, 17] His Torah teaching, based on making the Midrash accessible and preserving its text, made the Yalkut a foundational book without which no commentator, preacher or student of Torah can manage.[2, 3]
Rabbi Shimon's main contribution can be summed up along three central axes:
Rescue: the preservation of lost midrashim and of accurate versions of the literature of the Sages.[2]
Systematisation: the organisation of thousands of scattered sayings into a single exegetical sequence following the order of the Bible.[2, 7]
Continuity: the creation of a chain of generations of Torah scholars, from the Adler family to the present day, who draw from the depth of his homilies.[8, 12]
The Yalkut Shimoni stands today as a living testimony to the spirit of Frankfurt Jewry in the 13th century – a community that knew how to create and to rise above itself even in the shadow of persecutions, and to leave behind it an eternal spiritual treasure that enlightens the eyes of Israel to this very day.[2, 5, 6] Its scholarly and Torah importance only grows over the years, as more and more manuscripts are discovered and confirm the accuracy and depth of the "head of the preachers" in his sacred work.[2, 3, 8]
